# AN ITERATIVE ALGORITHM FOR COMPUTING THE BEST ESTIMATE OF AN ORTHOGONAL MATRIX*

A. BJÖRCK† AND C. BOWIE‡

Abstract. The closest unitary matrix, measured in Euclidean norm, to a given rectangular matrix $A$ is known to be the unitary factor in the polar decomposition of $A$ . The paper gives a family of iterative methods of order of convergence $p+1, p=1, 2, 3, \dots$ , for computing this matrix. The methods are especially efficient when the columns of $A$ are not too far from being orthonormal. The choice of order of convergence to minimize the amount of computation is discussed. Global convergence properties for the methods of order $\leq 4$ are studied and sufficient conditions for convergence in terms of $\| I - A^{H}A\|$ are given.

1. Introduction. Let A be a given $m\times n$ matrix with $m\geq n$ . Suppose that A can be represented as

$$
A = B + \delta B,
$$

where B is unitary, $B^{H}B=I_{n}$ , and $\delta B$ is a matrix of perturbations resulting from measurements, calculations or both. We consider here the problem of estimating B from the given matrix A.

Assume that the perturbations in the elements of A are independent random variables with constant variance. Then from the principle of least squares it seems reasonable to call $Q=P$ a best estimate of B if it minimizes $\| Q-A\|_{E}$ over all unitary m $\times$ n matrices Q. Here we have used the Euclidean or Forbenius norm of a matrix, viz.

$$
\| A \| _ {E} = \left(\sum_ {i, j} | a _ {i j} | ^ {2}\right) ^ {1 / 2}.
$$

We first introduce two matrix decompositions which play a significant role for the solution of this problem. It is well known (cf. [4]) that $A$ can be decomposed as

(1)

A = U D V ^ {H},

We first introduce two matrix decompositions which play a significant role for the solution of this problem. It is well known (cf. [4]) that $A$ can be decomposed as

(1)

$$
A = U D V ^ {H},
$$

where

$$
U ^ {H} U = V ^ {H} V = V V ^ {H} = I _ {n}, \quad D = \operatorname {d i a g} \left(\sigma_ {1}, \sigma_ {2}, \dots , \sigma_ {n}\right) \geq 0.
$$

Here $\sigma_{i}=\sigma_{i}(A)$ , the singular values of A, are the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^{H}A$ . We can always assume that

$$
\sigma_ {1} \geq \sigma_ {2} \geq \dots \geq \sigma_ {r} > \sigma_ {r + 1} = \dots = \sigma_ {n} = 0,
$$

r = rank (A).

From (1) it follows that we can write

$$
A = P H, \quad P = U V ^ {H}, \quad H = V D V ^ {H},
$$

(2)

where $P$ is unitary and $H$ positive semidefinite. This is known as the polar decom-

The significance of the polar decomposition is due to the following theorem.

THEOREM 1. Let $\mathcal{M}_{m,n}$ be the set of all m $\times$ n unitary matrices. For an arbitrary m $\times$ n matrix A let A = PH, where P $\in\mathcal{M}_{m,n}$ and H is Hermitian positive semi-definite. Then for any unitary matrix Q $\in\mathcal{M}_{m,n}$

$$
\| Q - A \| _ {E} \geq \| P - A \| _ {E}.
$$

This theorem was proved for $m=n$ and more general norms by Fan and Hoffman [3]. The generalization to $m>n$ follows easily from the additive property of $\| \cdot\|_{E}^{2}$ or alternatively from a theorem by Schonemann [8].

In the following we shall derive an iterative algorithm for computing the unitary factor in the polar decomposition of A. Since $H=P^{H}A$ , the algorithm can also be used when the whole polar decomposition is wanted.

2. The algorithm. Our method is based on the identity

(3)

$$
e ^ {i \varphi} = z \left(1 - \left(1 - | z | ^ {2}\right)\right) ^ {- 1 / 2},
$$

where $z=|z|e^{i\varphi}$ is a complex number. If we put $q=1-|z|^{2}$ and expand the right-hand side in Taylor series we get

$$
e ^ {i \varphi} = z \left(1 + \frac {1}{2} q + \frac {3}{8} q ^ {2} + \dots + (- 1) ^ {p} \binom {- \frac {1}{2}} {p} q ^ {p} + \dots\right).
$$

Using a well-known analogy between matrices and complex numbers we get from (3) the relation

$$
P = A \left(I - \left(I - A ^ {H} A\right)\right) ^ {- 1 / 2},
$$

Using a well-known analogy between matrices and complex numbers we get from (3) the relation

$$
P = A \left(I - \left(I - A ^ {H} A\right)\right) ^ {- 1 / 2},
$$

where P is the unitary matrix in the polar factorization of A. Thus we have the expansion

(4)

$$
P = A \left(I + \frac {1}{2} Q + \frac {3}{8} Q ^ {2} + \dots + (- 1) ^ {p} \binom {- \frac {1}{2}} {p} Q ^ {p} + \dots\right),
$$

where

$$
Q = I - A ^ {H} A.
$$

(5)

This matrix series converges if $\rho ( Q ) < 1$ , where $\rho ( Q )$ is the spectral radius of $Q.$ It can of course be used as it stands for computing P . However, by terminating the expansion after the term of order $Q^{p}$ , we can construct an iteration method of order p+1 as follows.

ALGORITHM. Put $A_{0}=A$ and compute $A_{1}, A_{2}, \dots$ recursively from

(6)

$$
A _ {k + 1} = A _ {k} \left(I + \frac {1}{2} Q _ {k} + \frac {3}{8} Q _ {k} ^ {2} + \dots + (- 1) ^ {p} \binom {- \frac {1}{2}} {p} Q _ {k} ^ {p}\right) = A _ {k} g _ {p} \left(Q _ {k}\right), \quad k \geq 0,
$$

p $\geq 1$ and

$$
Q _ {k} = I - A _ {k} ^ {H} A _ {k}.
$$

We shall prove that if $\rho (Q)$ is sufficiently small, then the sequence $A_{k}$ converges to P. We first show that the algorithm is unitarily invariant in a certain sense.

LEMMA 1. Let $A_{k}$ be defined by (6) and let U and V be arbitrary unitary matrices of dimension $m\times m$ and $n\times n$ respectively. If we put

$$
B _ {0} = U ^ {H} A _ {0} V, \quad B _ {k + 1} = B _ {k} g _ {p} \left(I - B _ {k} ^ {H} B _ {k}\right). \quad k \geq 0,
$$

then

(7)

$$
B _ {k} = U ^ {H} A _ {k} V, \quad k \geq 0.
$$

Proof. If (7) is true for some k, then

$$
B _ {k + 1} = U ^ {H} A _ {k} V g _ {p} \left(I - V ^ {H} A _ {k} ^ {H} A _ {k} V\right) = U ^ {H} A _ {k} V V ^ {H} g _ {p} \left(I - A _ {k} ^ {H} A _ {k}\right) V = U ^ {H} A _ {k + 1} V,
$$

and the lemma follows by complete induction.

THEOREM 2. Let $A_{k}$ be defined by (6) and let P be the unitary factor in the polar decomposition (2). Consider the corresponding scalar iteration

(8)

$$
z _ {k + 1} = z _ {k} g _ {p} \left(q _ {k}\right), \quad q _ {k} = 1 - \left| z _ {k} \right| ^ {2},
$$

$$
k \geq 0.
$$

Then for $A_{k}$ to converge to P it is necessary and sufficient that $z_{k}$ converge to 1 for all starting values

k \geq 0.
$$

$$
z _ {0} = \sigma_ {i} (A), \quad i = 1, 2, \dots , n.
$$

Proof. Let the singular value decomposition of A be

$$
A = U D _ {0} V ^ {H}, \quad D _ {0} = \operatorname {d i a g} \left(\sigma_ {i} (A)\right).
$$

Then from Lemma 1 it follows that $A_{k}= U D_{k} V^{H}$ , where the $D_{k}$ are real diagonal matrices and

$$
D _ {k + 1} = D _ {k} g _ {p} \left(I - D _ {k} ^ {2}\right),
$$

$$
k \geq 0.
$$

Now let $z_{k}$ be the i th element in $D_{k}.$ Then $z_{k}$ satisfies (8) and $z_{0}=\sigma_{i}(A).$ Since

$$
\lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} A _ {k} = U V ^ {H} = P \quad \mathrm {i f a n d o n l y i f} \quad \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} D _ {k} = I,
$$

the theorem follows.

We postpone the discussion of the global convergence of (8) to $\Sigma4.$ To find the order of the iteration method we square (6) and obtain

$$
A _ {k + 1} ^ {H} A _ {k + 1} = I - Q _ {k + 1} = \left(I - Q _ {k}\right) \left(I + \frac {1}{2} Q _ {k} + \dots + (- 1) ^ {p} \binom {- \frac {1}{2}} {p} Q _ {k} ^ {p}\right) ^ {2}
$$

or

or

$$
I - Q _ {k + 1} = \left(I - Q _ {k}\right) \left(\left(I - Q _ {k}\right) ^ {- 1 / 2} + (- 1) ^ {p + 1} \binom {- \frac {1}{2}} {p + 1} Q _ {k} ^ {p + 1} + O \left(Q _ {k} ^ {p + 2}\right)\right) ^ {2}.
$$

It follows that

$$
Q _ {k + 1} = 2 (- 1) ^ {p} \binom {- \frac {1}{2}} {p + 1} Q _ {k} ^ {p + 1} + O \left(Q _ {k} ^ {p + 2}\right).
$$

Using the relation $Q_{k} = (P + A_{k})^{H}(P - A_{k})$ we deduce that if $A_{k}$ converges to P, then

(9)

$$
\lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} \frac {\| P - A _ {k + 1} \| _ {2}}{\| P - A _ {k} \| _ {2} ^ {p + 1}} = (- 2) ^ {p + 1} \binom {- \frac {1}{2}} {p + 1}.
$$

Thus the order of convergence is $p+1.$

3. Choice of order. In many applications one iteration in (6) with $p=1$ will suffice to get the desired accuracy, i.e.,

$$
P \approx A \left(I + \frac {1}{2} Q\right), \quad Q = I - A ^ {H} A.
$$

However sometimes it may be advantageous to use $p > 1$ . We note that one iteration in (6) consists of the following three steps:

(ii)

$$
\begin{array}{l} Q _ {k} = I - A _ {k} ^ {H} A _ {k}, \quad \frac {1}{2} m n ^ {2} \text {m u l t i p l i c a t i o n s}, \\ E _ {k} = g _ {p} \left(Q _ {k}\right), \quad \frac {1}{2} (p - 1) n ^ {3} \text {m u l t i p l i c a t i o n s}, \\ A _ {k + 1} = A _ {k} E _ {k}, \quad m n ^ {2} \text {m u l t i p l i c a t i o n s}, \\ \end{array}
$$

(iii)

We have given the number of multiplications required for each step. Thus the total amount of work in one step is proportional to

(10)

$$
w _ {p} = \frac {3}{2} m n ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2} (p - 1) n ^ {3}.
$$

(10) $$ w _ {p} = \frac {3}{2} m n ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2} (p - 1) n ^ {3}. $$ We have assumed that $g_{p} \left( Q_{k} \right)$ is evaluated using Horner's rule. It has been shown by Ostrowski [7] that for scalar polynomials there is no scheme with fewer multiplications for $p \leq 4.$ For larger p it is certainly possible to decrease the second term in (10), but we shall disregard this here. We first note that since $w_{p}$ is not much greater than $w_{1}$ for $p=[m/n]$ , a large value of $p$ may be useful when $m\gg n$ . Another interesting special case is $m=n$ Then $w_{p}=\frac{1}{2} n^{3}(p+2)$ and since the order of convergence is $p+1$ we can use as efficiency index [9] for the iteration, $$ \varkappa_ {p} = \frac {1}{p + 2} \log (p + 1). $$ In order to minimize the number of multiplications for a fixed reduction of the error, we should maximize $\varkappa_{p}$ . Since the $\sigma_{i} ( A )$ are not known this is not immediately useful. However from the relation $A^{H} A=I-Q$ it follows that $\sigma_{i}^{2}(A)=1-\lambda_{i}(Q)$ , or for any consistent matrix norm,

(13)

$$
\left| \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (A) - 1 \right| \leq \rho (Q) \leq \| Q \|, \quad i = 1, 2, \dots
$$

This is used below to derive easily checked sufficient conditions for convergence.

This is used below to derive easily checked sufficient conditions for convergence.

THEOREM 3a. Let $A_{k}$ be defined by (6) with $p\leq 3.$ If rank $( A)=n,$ and if, for some consistent matrix norm,

$$
\| Q \| < d _ {p} ^ {2} - 1,
$$

lim $k \to \infty$ A<sub>k</sub> = P.

Proof. Since rank $( A )=n$ it follows that $0<\sigma_{i} ( A ).$ From (13) we have that $\sigma_{i}^{2}(A)<1+d_{p}^{2}-1=d_{p}^{2}.$ Thus also the right inequality in (12) is satisfied, which concludes the proof.

We also give a corresponding theorem without the assumption on the rank of A.

THEOREM 3b. Let $A_{k}$ be defined by (6) with $p\leq 3.$ If, for some consistent matrix norm,

$$
\| Q \| < 1,
$$

$\lim_{k \to \infty} A_k = P.$

Proof. From (13) we have that $\sigma_{n}^{2}(A)>1-\| Q\|>0$ , and thus rank $( A)=n.$ Convergence now follows from Theorem 3a since for $p\leq 3$ it is true that $d_{p}^{2}-1\geq 1.$

We remark that if $\sigma_{i} ( A ) > d_{p}$ for some i, then we may get convergence to a nonoptimal unitary matrix. For example, if p = 1 and $z_{0}=2$ in (8), then $z_{n}=-1$ for n > 0. Thus, when $0 < \sigma_{i} ( A )\leq 2$ , the corresponding matrix iteration converges to a matrix $U D V^{H}$ , which is unitary since $D^{2}=I$ , but may differ from $U V^{H}$ No improvement of Theorems 3a and 3b will therefore be attempted.

Some convenient norms to use in the theorems above are

$$
\| Q \| _ {E} = \left(\sum_ {i, j} | q _ {i j} | ^ {2}\right) ^ {1 / 2}, \quad \| Q \| _ {1} = \max _ {i} \sum_ {j} | q _ {i j} |, \quad \| Q \| _ {M} = n \max _ {i, j} | q _ {i j} |.
$$

Note that $\| Q\|_{E}$ and $\| Q\|_{1}$ both give sharper bounds than $\| Q\|_{M}$ , since we always have $\| Q\|_{E}\leq\| Q\|_{M}$ and $\| Q\|_{1}\leq\| Q\|_{M}.$

5. Remarks. Another possible way to obtain $P$ would be to compute the singular value decomposition (1) of A. An efficient algorithm for this has recently been developed by Golub and Reinsch [5], and a FORTRAN program for the complex case is found in [2]. This algorithm requires, however, approximately $10mn^{2}$ multiplications. When A is reasonably close to a unitary matrix our algorithm will require much less work.

A special type of problem in which the algorithm has proved to be very efficient is illustrated by the following. Suppose that the differential equations describing the motion of a missile are to be solved by a step-wise procedure. One of the items of interest is the matrix M of transformation between an orthogonal axis system fixed with respect to the missile and an inertial system. Assuming that care is exercised in setting the initial conditions, M is certainly orthogonal at the outset. However, computational errors are unavoidable when M is updated at every time step. If no precautions are taken, M may have drifted considerably away from orthogonality after a hundred steps. It is therefore prudent to adjust M after a fixed small number of steps. Since M is always nearly orthogonal, one step of (6) with $p=1$ will suffice. A hardly different problem is discussed in [1]; the procedure suggested there is inferior to that proposed here.

We finally point out that in many cases it may not be essential to get the best orthogonal approximation in the sense used here. Then one can apply instead the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process to the columns of A. This will yield (disregarding rounding errors) an exactly orthogonal matrix with the same column space as A using only $m n^{2}$ multiplications and no extra memory space. A variation of this scheme is suggested in [6]. In this situation our method

cannot compete since even only one iteration with $p=1$ will require $\frac{3}{2} m n^{2}$ operation and $\frac{1}{2} n^{2}$ extra memory locations.
